value.overview: The White-winged Becard (Pachyramphus polychopterus) is a small to medium-sized songbird of the family Tityridae. It has a broad distribution from Central America through much of tropical South America. Males and females look notably different: males are mainly black, gray, and white, while females are olive-brown and buff. The species usually lives high in trees, where it searches foliage for insects and occasionally takes fruit.
value.classification: The White-winged Becard belongs to the order Passeriformes and family Tityridae, which includes becards, tityras, and related birds. Several geographic forms are recognized across its wide range.
value.identification: This becard has a relatively large, broad head, a short bill, and a compact body. The adult male is mostly black above with gray underparts and conspicuous white markings on the wings, including broad white edges or wingbars. The female is duller, with olive-brown upperparts, pale grayish or buff underparts, and contrasting pale wing markings. Its habit of perching quietly in the middle or upper canopy can make it easier to detect by its calls than by sight.
value.rangeHabitat: The White-winged Becard ranges from southern Mexico and Central America through northern and central South America, including the Amazon Basin and parts of the Atlantic Forest region. In Costa Rica it occurs on both the Pacific and Caribbean slopes and is found in lowlands and foothills, especially in open woodland, forest edges, clearings with scattered trees, second-growth vegetation, and sometimes gardens or plantations. It generally favors structurally varied habitats rather than the darkest interior of mature forest, and often forages from the middle levels to the upper canopy.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally regarded as resident or locally dispersive across its range. In Costa Rica, it occurs year-round on both slopes; substantial long-distance migration is not normally expected, although local movements may follow food availability or seasonal conditions.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding has been recorded mainly from late March or April through August, during the wetter part of the year. The nest is a bulky, enclosed or globular structure with a side entrance, built from plant fibers and other soft materials and placed in a tree, usually well above the ground. The female performs most incubation, while both parents feed the nestlings. Young typically leave the nest at about three weeks of age.
value.dietFeeding: The White-winged Becard feeds mainly on insects and other arthropods, including beetles, grasshoppers, caterpillars, and insect larvae. It usually watches from a leafy perch and makes short darts to seize prey from foliage or nearby airspace. Fruit and other small plant foods may supplement the diet, particularly when insects are less abundant. Adults commonly forage alone, in pairs, or occasionally with mixed-species feeding groups.
value.behavior: This becard is usually quiet and inconspicuous while moving through the canopy, often sitting upright on exposed or leafy branches before making a quick feeding flight. It commonly occurs singly or in pairs and defends a breeding territory through soft, repeated songs and calls. The sexes may look so different that they can be mistaken for separate species. Nesting birds can be persistent and attentive, with both parents contributing to care of the young.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly established, but the species is not currently considered globally threatened.
